notes: Full commercial court judgment on arbitration clause scope and anti-suit injunction against Finnish proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: P&I club anti-suit injunction where Finnish direct-action claim is subject to London arbitration
key_facts: After a container of garments was lost on a through transport leg through Russia, New India (having taken assignment from the cargo insurer) pursued the TT Club in Finland under section 67 of the Finnish Insurance Contracts Act 1994.
The Club's rules contained a wide London arbitration clause and indemnity/pay-to-be-paid terms governed by English law.
The Club commenced English proceedings for declarations and an anti-suit injunction; the Kotka District Court held New India was not bound by the arbitration clause.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside service out of the jurisdiction and to stay English proceedings, opposed by the Club's application for an anti-suit injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Service out upheld; stay under Article 27 refused; anti-suit injunction granted restraining New India from continuing the Finnish proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Where a direct-action claim against an insurer is in substance enforcement of contractual indemnity governed by English law, the English court will characterise it as a claim on obligation and hold the claimant bound by the arbitration agreement, notwithstanding a foreign statutory right of direct action.
legal_issues: Whether New India's Finnish direct-action claim was subject to the Club's arbitration clause
Whether Article 27 of the Brussels Regulation required a stay of the English proceedings
Whether an anti-suit injunction should issue to restrain proceedings in another EU member state

notes: Long admiralty trial judgment finding fraudulent engine representations on sale of motor yacht Brave Challenger.

enrichment.short_title: Buyers' misrepresentation claim over falsely represented Proteus engine overhauls on yacht sale
key_facts: In April 2000 Ronastone and the Succession Trust trustees bought the motor yacht Brave Challenger from Indigo and Urbane for £2 million, with £1.3 million secured by mortgage.
Sellers represented that three Proteus gas turbine engines had been properly overhauled; expert evidence indicated at least one engine had far more running time and overhaul claims were fraudulent.
Parallel in rem mortgage enforcement (Folio 411) and in personam rescission/damages proceedings (Folio 518) followed prolonged disputes over documentation and vessel condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated admiralty trial of sellers' in rem mortgage claim and buyers' in personam misrepresentation counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Buyers established inducing misrepresentation as to engine condition; entitled to damages under the Misrepresentation Act 1967; vessel valued at about £750,000 at sale date with further consequential loss to be argued.
enrichment.ratio: Representations that main engines had been overhauled to manufacturer standards induced the purchase despite an 'as is where is' clause, and sellers failed to prove reasonable belief in the truth of those representations.
legal_issues: Whether sellers misrepresented the condition and overhaul status of the Proteus engines
Whether buyers relied on oral and written representations despite limited inspection
Whether an 'as is where is' term excluded implied terms and rescission
Measure of damages for fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation

notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment dismissing conviction appeal after trial in absentia for large-scale money laundering.

enrichment.short_title: Trial in absentia upheld after £6.2m bureau de change money laundering conviction
key_facts: The appellant was convicted in his absence at Leicester Crown Court of three conspiracies to launder about £6.2m of sterling exchanged for Dutch guilders at London bureaux de change.
He disappeared the day before trial, was convicted with counsel continuing to act, and later claimed he had been abducted and held in Belgium for nearly three months.
Co-defendants pleaded guilty shortly after his disappearance, casting him as principal conspirator.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and applications for leave to appeal against sentence after trial conducted in the appellant's absence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; all applications for leave to appeal against conviction refused; abduction account rejected as incapable of belief.
enrichment.ratio: An indictment alleging conspiracy to launder proceeds of drug trafficking and/or other criminal conduct is not bad for duplicity under section 1(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1977, and 'knowing or having reasonable grounds to suspect' in particulars mirroring substantive offences is an immaterial averment where the real issue is agreement to launder illicit money.
legal_issues: Duplicity and uncertainty of money-laundering conspiracy counts
Whether 'reasonable grounds to suspect' suffices for statutory conspiracy mens rea
Fairness and safety of trial in voluntary absence
Admissibility of fresh evidence of alleged abduction under section 23

notes: Court of Appeal re-exercise of discretion on lifting CPR Part 51 automatic stays in North Wales abuse negligence claims.

enrichment.short_title: Lifting CPR Part 51 automatic stays in North Wales child abuse solicitor negligence claims
key_facts: Four claimants sued solicitors Rex Makin (and counsel in one action) for advising they could not pursue local authority child abuse claims in North Wales.
Actions commenced in 1999 were automatically stayed under CPR Part 51 because they were not brought before the court between April 1999 and April 2000.
Applications to lift the stay in 2002 were refused by Master Ungley and on appeal; Simon Brown LJ granted permission on whether fair-trial risk was required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to lift automatic stays imposed under CPR Part 51 transitional provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; automatic stays lifted on stringent terms; Master’s discretion re-exercised in claimants' favour.
enrichment.ratio: Relief from a CPR Part 51 automatic stay under CPR 3.9 does not require proof of a substantial risk that a fair trial is impossible; all circumstances including double discounting of prospects if claims are finally barred must be weighed, and limited prejudice from litigation hanging over defendants may not justify refusal.
legal_issues: Application of CPR 3.9 factors to Part 51 automatic stays
Whether Taylor v Anderson fair-trial impossibility test applies
Prejudice to professional defendants from delay versus claimants' loss if stays not lifted
Correct construction of CPR 3.9 sub-rules in transitional stay cases

notes: Chancery trial on construction of land purchase option extended by planning delay tactics.

enrichment.short_title: Developer validly extended cinema site option despite keeping first planning application in abeyance

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Development Procedure) Order 1995

key_facts: The Morris brothers granted Glendore an option to buy a West Ealing cinema/snooker site for £1.32m, with the option period extendable under a third schedule if planning applications remained undetermined.
Glendore submitted a first planning application before the initial termination date, then kept it in abeyance while pursuing parallel applications with a housing association.
The brothers argued Glendore acted in bad faith to delay decisions and forfeited extension rights; Glendore exercised the option in January 2003 after the first application was finally refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of claim that option had expired and counterclaim for specific performance and loan repayment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; counterclaims for specific performance and recovery of £142,250 advanced for lease surrender succeeded.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 1 of the third schedule extends the option until 98 days after written receipt of a decision on a qualifying pre-deadline application; delaying local authority determination without a section 78(2) agreement does not automatically terminate the option where the application remains live and Glendore acted in good faith using a recognised twin-tracking planning strategy.
legal_issues: Construction of option extension provisions in the third schedule
Whether Glendore breached implied good faith or purpose limitations
Effect of non-determination within eight weeks without a section 78(2) agreement
Estoppel by acquiescence to parallel planning applications

notes: Court of Appeal affirming FSCS liability for employer's defence costs under compulsory insurance policy.

enrichment.short_title: FSCS must indemnify employer's pre-liquidation defence costs under compulsory EL policy
key_facts: Geologistics held a composite business liability policy with Independent Insurance including employers' liability cover; an employee successfully sued for about £110,000 plus costs.
Independent went into provisional liquidation during the appeal; Geologistics paid DAC about £15,700 in pre-liquidation defence costs and sought reimbursement from the FSCS.
The Scheme accepted liability for damages and the employee's costs but denied liability for Geologistics' own defence costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Davis J's judgment in judicial review proceedings granting declaratory relief that the FSCS must pay pre-liquidation defence costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; FSCS liable to indemnify Geologistics for defence costs incurred before liquidation, subject to policy terms.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 6(4)-(5) of the Policyholders Protection Act 1975, 'in respect of a liability subject to compulsory insurance' covers policy liabilities connected with compulsory insurance, including defence costs under general policy extensions, and section 6(5) excludes only liabilities unrelated to such compulsory cover.
legal_issues: Construction of 'in respect of' in section 6(5) of the 1975 Act
Whether defence costs are covered where claimant's costs are accepted as recoverable
Purpose of section 6 as protecting corporate compulsory policyholders at 100%
Relationship between sections 6(4), 6(5) and 6(6)

notes: Planning s.287 challenge quashing increased North Bersted housing allocation in adopted local plan.

enrichment.short_title: North Bersted SITE6 housing allocation quashed for inquiry and infrastructure review failures

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Arun District Council adopted its 2003 local plan including policy SITE6 allocating 650 dwellings at North Bersted, increased from 350 after the inspector recommended at least 300 additional homes subject to infrastructure review.
Bersted Parish Council objected that no second inquiry was held on the modified allocation and that infrastructure implications were not reviewed before adoption.
The council deferred and then effectively foreclosed consideration of a further inquiry, relying on mistaken legal advice that earlier stages could not be revisited.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 287 application to quash part of the adopted Arun District Local Plan 2003 relating to North Bersted under policy SITE6.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; relevant part of the local plan quashed; council's errors on second inquiry consideration and infrastructure precondition were material.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority must properly consider whether to hold a further inquiry into objections to proposed modifications under regulation 29, taking into account all relevant Drexfine/Warren factors including fairness; where an inspector conditionally recommended increased housing subject to prior infrastructure review, adopting the higher figure without that review misinterprets the inspector's report and exceeds planning powers.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of refusing a second local plan inquiry into SITE6 modifications
Whether infrastructure review was a precondition to increasing the North Bersted allocation
Exercise of discretion to grant section 287 relief
Correct application of CPR/development plan regulations to proposed modifications

notes: Construction appeal on IChemE termination certificate expert jurisdiction after clause 11 amendment.

enrichment.short_title: IChemE expert may revise provisional termination certificate and order prompt payment
key_facts: Rhodia terminated a piping sub-contract with Laker Vent under IChemE model form clause 43; the project manager issued a provisional termination certificate deducting £100,000 retention.
Laker Vent referred disputes to an IChemE expert; Rhodia argued amended clause 11 routed all disputes to arbitration under clause 46 and denied the expert power to order payment.
The expert revised the certificate and directed payment; Rhodia's newly appointed project manager later issued a final certificate including a large remedial works set-off.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two linked appeals from summary judgment orders in the Technology and Construction Court enforcing expert decisions on retention and further termination sums.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; expert had jurisdiction; summary judgment upheld for sums due under revised provisional termination certificate.
enrichment.ratio: Amending the agreement to refer disputes to clause 46 did not exclude expert determination under clause 45 where clause 46 is expressly subject to clause 45 and clause 43.9 requires expert resolution of provisional certificate disputes; an expert's decision revises the provisional certificate and triggers prompt payment under clause 43.10, distinct from final certification.
legal_issues: Whether clause 11 amendment excluded expert determination under clause 45
Whether Rhodia submitted to the expert's jurisdiction
Extent of expert powers under clauses 43.9 and 45.2 to revise provisional certificates and order payment
Effect of a belated final termination certificate on enforcement of provisional certificate decisions

notes: Lead flip-flop CGT appeal allowing taxpayers' construction of section 77 derived property.

enrichment.short_title: Flip-flop CGT scheme succeeds where borrowed cash in second settlement is not derived property
key_facts: Former Einkorn Ltd shareholders used twin settlements: shares transferred to a first settlement on hold-over, cash borrowed against the shares and appointed to a second settlement, then the settlor was excluded before the shares were sold.
The Revenue argued section 77(2) treated the settlor as having an interest in the first settlement because cash in the second settlement was 'derived property' of the charged shares.
Special Commissioners allowed the appeals; Peter Smith J allowed the Revenue's appeal on derived property.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Lead appeal (Trennery) with four consolidated appeals from High Court decision on section 77(8) derived property.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; cash transferred to the second settlement was not derived property after leaving the first settlement; settlor not chargeable under section 77 on the gain.
enrichment.ratio: 'Derived property' in section 77(8) covers income and settled property representing proceeds of source property while it remains comprised in the chargeable settlement; property that leaves the settlement ceases to be derived property, so a settlor's interest in a separate second settlement is irrelevant to section 77(2).
legal_issues: Construction of 'derived property' in section 77(8) TCGA 1992
Whether borrowed cash appointed to a second settlement remained derived property of shares in the first settlement
Interaction of sections 77(2)(a) and (b) and section 79 source-property rules
Whether 1995 amendments extended section 77 beyond the chargeable settlement's confines

enrichment.short_title: Children ordered returned to Germany despite objections after unlawful half-term retention

statutes_considered.title: Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980

key_facts: Two Australian children habitually resident in Germany with their father were retained in England by their mother after an agreed October 2003 half-term contact visit.
A February 2002 consent order had placed residence with the father in Germany for three years; German custody proceedings were pending when the mother refused return.

Both children objected to returning, citing school difficulties, strained relationship with the father, and fear of losing contact with the mother; JA had recently learned the father was not his biological parent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Hague Convention summary return application under the Child Abduction and Custody Act 1985.
enrichment.outcome: Return to Germany ordered; Article 13(b) grave risk defence rejected; children's objections acknowledged but discretion exercised in favour of return with undertakings on support and prosecution immunity.
enrichment.ratio: Children's objections under Article 13 may be outweighed where retention was unlawful, habitual residence and pending German proceedings favour return, objections intensified after wrongful retention and maternal influence, and undertakings adequately address grave risk and welfare pending German determination.
legal_issues: Whether children objected with sufficient maturity for Article 13 discretion
Grave risk of harm or intolerable situation under Article 13(b)
Exercise of discretion where objections conflict with Convention objectives
Effect of pending German custody and relocation proceedings
